DH reminds public to take precautions against heat-related illnesses during very hot weather
The Centre for Health Protection (CHP) of the Department of Health (DH) today (September 19) reminded members of the public to take appropriate precautions against heat-related illnesses, such as heat cramps, heat exhaustion and heat stroke, during very hot weather.
In a high-temperature environment, excessive sweating and difficulty in heat dissipation can cause stress to the body. Members of the public should take the following precautions:
- Hydrate in a timely manner to prevent dehydration;
- Wear light-coloured, loose-fitting and breathable clothing to minimise heat absorption and facilitate perspiration and heat dissipation;
- Keep indoor areas well ventilated and maintain appropriate temperature and humidity, e.g. by opening windows or using a fan or air-conditioning;
- Avoid strenuous exercise and prolonged activities such as hiking or trekking;
- Arrange outdoor activities in the morning or the late afternoon, if possible, and bring enough water; and
- Avoid beverages containing caffeine, such as coffee and tea, as well as alcoholic beverages, which may speed up water loss through the urinary system.
In addition, infants and children, the elderly, pregnant women, individuals with chronic illnesses such as heart disease or high blood pressure, overweight people and outdoor/manual workers are more susceptible to heat stroke. These groups should pay special attention to the following:
- Infants and young children: Avoid going outside when the temperature is high. If they must go outside, adults should ensure they stay in places with moderate temperatures and good ventilation or air-conditioning. Infants and young children should never be left unattended in a confined space such as a vehicle;
- The elderly, pregnant women, individuals with chronic illnesses and overweight people: Pay close attention to health conditions and seek help as soon as possible if experiencing any abnormalities in health indicators such as blood pressure, heart rate, etc or if there are fluctuations in health conditions. Avoid going out when the temperature is high. Make sure there is good ventilation, or turn on a fan or air-conditioner to keep an appropriate temperature indoors. High temperatures can also worsen the condition of people with chronic illnesses (such as cardiovascular and respiratory diseases). Therefore, they should have an ample supply of their usual medication and keep in contact with family members, neighbours and the community. People should seek immediate help if they feel unwell.
- Outdoor/manual workers: Reschedule work to cooler hours as far as feasible. If working in a hot environment is unavoidable, provide shade where practicable and use ventilation and heat dissipation equipment. Once work has begun, gradually adjust the pace of work and take breaks in the shade to regain strength.
The DH reminded the public that heat stroke is one of the most common health risks in hot weather. Over the past five years, there have been over 200 hospital admissions due to heat stroke each year in Hong Kong, with two to five fatal cases occurring mainly during the summer months from May to September. Vulnerable groups are more susceptible to heat stroke. Symptoms include dizziness, headache, nausea, shortness of breath or confusion. In severe cases, patients may suffer from convulsions or become unconscious, which can be life-threatening if they are not cooled down and resuscitated in a timely manner.
Members of the public are also advised to pay attention to the latest weather, as well as the real-time and forecasted ultraviolet (UV) index released by the Hong Kong Observatory (HKO). When the UV index is high (6 or above), the public should note the following:
- Avoid direct sunlight exposure to the skin and the eyes;
- Apply broad-spectrum, water-resistant sunscreen liberally, with a sun protection factor (SPF) of at least 30 or higher, when participating in outdoor activities. Reapply every two hours if staying outdoors for long periods, or after swimming, sweating or towelling off;
- While using DEET-containing insect repellents for personal protection against mosquito-borne diseases, apply sunscreen before insect repellent;
If symptoms develop, such as dizziness, headache, nausea, shortness of breath or confusion, rest and seek help immediately, and seek medical advice as soon as possible.
For more health information, the public may visit theCHP's heat strokepage andUV radiation page; the HKO's Dial-a-Weather (1878 200),latestweather report and forecast,UV Indexand weather information forhiking and mountaineering; andpress releasesof the Labour Departmenton precautions against heat stroke for outdoor workers and their employers when the Heat Stress at Work Warning is in force.

LegCo Subcommittee to Study Matters Relating to "Ecology + Tourism" visits Wong Chuk Kok Tsui, Tung Ping Chau and Yan Chau Tong of Hong Kong UNESCO Global Geopark
The following is issued on behalf of the Legislative Council Secretariat:
The Legislative Council (LegCo) Subcommittee to Study Matters Relating to "Ecology + Tourism" visited Wong Chuk Kok Tsui, Tung Ping Chau and Yan Chau Tong of the Hong Kong UNESCO Global Geopark (Hong Kong Geopark) by boat today (September 19) to gain a deeper understanding of Government measures relating to the conservation of landforms and marine ecology there, and to explore how to further promote island tourism.
Accompanied by the Director of Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation, Mr Mickey Lai, the Assistant Commissioner for Tourism, Miss Agnes Ho, and other representatives of the Government, LegCo Members set sail from Tseng Tau Pier to inspect the geological features and marine ecology in the Northeast New Territories Sedimentary Rock Region of the Hong Kong Geopark. The boat first passed Wong Chuk Kok Tsui, the oldest stratum in Hong Kong formed approximately 400 million years ago, and Mirs Bay, which was selected as a national "Outstanding Example of Beautiful Bays". Members also received a briefing from representatives of relevant departments on conservation and recreational measures in the vicinity of the Northeast New Territories, tourism promotion efforts and water quality in Mirs Bay. Members suggested reviewing the mechanism of professional training and licensing relating to eco-tourism, to equip more tourism industry practitioners with the relevant knowledge to tell visitors the stories of Hong Kong's natural environment and culture.
Members continued the boat journey to Tung Ping Chau, where they viewed from offshore its unique geo-attractions, such as the wave-cut platform, the rock columns named Kang Lau Shek. After landing on the island, Members inspected the geological features, ecological environment and auxiliary facilities near the pier, and learnt about the Tung Ping Chau Pier works. Members exchanged views with representatives of the Government on ways to further enhance the pier's facilities to promote island tourism more effectively.
During the visit, Members received a briefing from the Government on the island's geology and ecology, which supports over 60 hard coral species as well as a wide variety of marine invertebrates and reef fish. To strengthen conservation efforts at Tung Ping Chau, the Government designated Tung Ping Chau as a marine park and has prohibited fishing and mooring in surrounding waters.
Members also viewed Yan Chau Tong, Lai Chi Wo, Crooked Island and Ap Chau from the boat. Members learned about the landforms of the area and the long history of Hakka and fishing communities, and exchanged views with representatives of the Government on leveraging the unique natural resources to better develop rural and island tourism.
A total of 13 members and non-members of the Subcommittee participated in the visit.

NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WTVF) — Shakespeare in the Park...or Shakespeare in the Heat?
The Nashville Shakespeare Festival organizers are pushing back the last 'Shakespeare in the Park' performances to be closer to when the sun sets. An ongoing heat advisory prompted the adjustment.
"It's really...really, really hot," said Susan Hammonds-White, a frequent visitor of the shows. "Like a weighted blanket that's full of coals. It's just very hot!"
While Hammonds-White said the temperatures are the worst they've ever been, the festival's executive director, Isabel Tipton-Krispin, said the team has been through worse.
"We've had rain, Hurricane Helene, heat indexes being high..." she started. "So you know, it just runs the gamut, and that's just part of outdoor theater."
The heat is also not dissuading people from showing out. Tipton-Krispin said they're seeing their biggest audiences as of late, reaching close to 9,000 people this year.
The remaining 'A Midsummer Night's Dream' performances in Centennial Park will now be at 7:30 p.m. for the rest of the weekend.
Gates will open at 6 p.m., and the pre-show concert starts at 6:30 p.m.

But merely counting deaths from heat risks missing its impact on human life. Each heat dome in the U.S. affected over 100 million people. Among them were construction workers, outdoor workers, delivery workers in unairconditioned cabs, farm workers, the unhoused, the poor who could not afford air conditioning, those on medications on whom the impact of heat was amplified, those with mental health disorders, and those with little or no access to healthcare.
According to the International Labor Organization, billions of workers around the world are exposed to extreme heat every year. While the vast majority of them do not die, many suffer deeply from the arduous ignominy of a life exposed to heat, day and night, year after year.
While counting deaths from heat is an imperfect science, the quantification of heat’s impact on mental health, physical well-being, wages, food security, habitat, and infrastructure is even more complex. One thousand women working in India’s informal labor economy have set out to quantify this burden—to understand what impact the heat and humidity in their lived environments at home and at work have on their health, wages, and well-being.
